p.src: First, in popular editions, particles such as zhi, hu, zhe, and ye are for the most part misplaced and unintelligible; the language is also prolix and often repetitive. These have now all been corrected according to the old edition, making the text considerably more direct and vigorous.

p.src: Second, popular editions contain many errors in their accounts of events. Examples include Xuande dropping his chopsticks upon hearing thunder, Ma Teng being killed after entering the capital, and Lord Guan being enfeoffed as Marquis of Hanshou Village; all these differ from the old edition. Moreover, Cao’s denunciation of Cao Pi is related in detail in Fan Ye’s Book of the Later Han, yet the popular edition wrongly portrays him instead as an accomplice in evil; and Lady Sun’s death by casting herself into the river is described in detail in the Biography of the Fierce Princess, whereas the popular edition merely records her return to Wu. These matters have now all been determined according to the old edition.

p.src: Third, certain indispensable episodes—Lord Guan holding a candle until dawn, Guan Ning cutting the mat and sitting apart, Cao Cao distributing incense and arranging for the sale of his remaining footwear, Yu Jin seeing his portrait in the imperial mausoleum, as well as the talent of the Marquis Wu’s wife, the wit of Zheng Kangcheng’s maidservant, Deng Ai’s response concerning the phoenix, Zhong Hui’s answer that he was not sweating, and Du Yu’s passion for the Zuo Commentary—are all deleted and omitted from the popular editions. These have now all been preserved according to the old edition, so that readers may glimpse the whole leopard from its markings.

p.src: Fourth, among the finest writings of the Three Kingdoms period are pieces included in the Selections of Refined Literature, such as Kong Rong’s Memorial Recommending Mi Heng and Chen Lin’s Proclamation Denouncing Cao Cao. These truly deserve to be transmitted alongside the earlier and later Memorials on Dispatching the Troops, yet popular editions omit them entirely. They have now all been added from the old edition, for the perusal of those who delight in antiquity.

p.src: Fifth, the chapter headings in popular editions are uneven and lack parallelism, being disorderly and without structure; moreover, a single chapter is divided into an upper and a lower section. They have now all been joined together in accordance with the author’s intent. Each chapter is headed by two parallel phrases, carefully polished to delight the reader’s eye.

p.src: Sixth, popular editions falsely claim to have been read and annotated by Master Li Zhuowu, though in the end no one knows whose hand the annotations actually came from; many of their comments affront Xuande and revile the Marquis Wu. All such passages have now been removed and replaced with newly written, corrected commentary.

p.src: Seventh, what is most laughable in popular editions is that they mark approving circles beside events deemed right and blot out those deemed wrong. If one judges the events rather than the writing, then since the Spring and Autumn Annals records thirty-six regicides and fifty-two ruined states, must one blot out the Sage’s entire classic? In the passages reviewed and annotated in this edition, there are circles but no obliterations, sweeping away the former vulgar practice.

p.src: Eighth, interspersing poetry and song lyrics within a narrative is one of the finest features of literary composition. Yet in popular editions, whenever the words “A later poet sighed in verse” appear, the author is invariably Master Zhou Jingxuan, and his poems are exceedingly vulgar and laughable. In the present edition, these have all been replaced with genuine works by renowned poets of the Tang and Song dynasties, making it entirely different from the popular editions.

p.src: Ninth, regulated verse in seven-character lines began with the poets of the Tang; no such seven-character regulated verse is known from the Han dynasty. Popular editions repeatedly fabricate poems by men of antiquity: Zhong Yao’s and Wang Lang’s odes to the Bronze Bird Terrace, and Cai Mao’s inscription on the wall of a posthouse, for example, are all forged in the form of seven-character regulated verse and are rightly ridiculed by the knowledgeable. These have now all been removed in accordance with the old edition, so as to preserve historical truth.

p.src: Tenth, among the stories fabricated by later generations are some absent from the popular Romance but found in present-day stage plays, such as Lord Guan beheading Diaochan and Zhang Fei capturing Zhou Yu. Their falsehood is known to people today. Others are absent from the old edition of the Records of the Three Kingdoms but found in the popular Romance, such as Zhuge Liang’s attempt to burn Wei Yan in the Upper Valley and Zhuge Zhan’s hesitation and indecision after receiving Deng Ai’s letter. Their falsehood, however, is not known to people today. If their falsehood goes unrecognized, does this not grievously wrong the people of old? These passages have now all been removed, so that readers will not be misled by the fanciful tales of Qi’s eastern countrymen.
